title: Explaining expenses and flagging payments for review
summary: I analysed 247,785 payment records, compared expenditure across equivalent periods and flagged 281 potential duplicate payment pairs worth £4.45m for Accounts Payable review.
scenario_note: The published data, analysis and findings are real. The workplace brief and stakeholder conversations are simulated to show how I would approach the task within a finance team.
brief: During a finance meeting, I was asked to analyse expenditure trends and identify potential duplicate payments. To ensure the report was relevant, I first confirmed the reporting period and the required focus: cash payments, budget performance, or outstanding commitments.
questions: Could ‘higher expenditure’ mean more cash paid, an overspend against a budget, or an increase in outstanding commitments?
Each question needs different records. Payment data shows cash outflow; it does not establish budget performance or committed costs.
The report would compare cash payments over equivalent dates and identify exceptions for investigation. Budget and commitment reporting would need additional data.
data_intro: Within the organisation, I would request authorised extracts from Finance and Accounts Payable (AP), agreeing the required fields and access before starting. For this project, I used Birmingham City Observatory’s published payments over £500, covering July 2024 to 23 July 2026.
data_requests: Payment dates, amounts, departments and credits establish expenditure trends.
Published payment records supplied these fields.
Supplier identifiers and names support supplier reporting and duplicate checks.
Published names and identifiers supported screening; the internal supplier master was unavailable.
Invoice and credit references distinguish repeated invoices from legitimate payments.
Not published. The findings remain a review list for AP.
Budgets, purchase orders and unpaid commitments support budget-performance reporting.
Not available here; excluded from the report’s scope.
etl_intro: I built an ETL workflow: extract the published records, transform inconsistent fields, then load a SQL reporting model. This kept the cleaning rules separate from the queries and Excel outputs.
mapping_intro: Department names changed during a restructure. For example, ‘Adults Social Care Directorate’ and ‘Adult Social Care & Health Directorate’ both needed to report under ‘Adult Social Care & Health’. Comparing the original labels could make spending appear to disappear from one department and emerge in another. I standardised the names as shown in the table below.
corporate_note: I also combined Council Management, Finance, HR, OD & Transformation, and Strategy, Insight & Governance into ‘Corporate services (combined)’ for the year-on-year comparison. The restructure moved budgets between these departments, so separate comparisons could mistake organisational changes for changes in spending.
validation_note: The cleaning script checks that every department has a mapping, the payment-line count stays unchanged, and the total payment value is preserved within one penny. These checks catch dropped records or altered amounts before reporting.
spending_intro: The export ended on 23 July 2026. I compared 1 April to 23 July in both years, so a partial July was not compared with a full month. Net payments rose from £558.64m to £677.46m: an increase of £118.82m, or 21.3%.
spending_interpretation: City Operations and Adult Social Care & Health made the largest positive contributions to the increase. Lower payments in corporate services and City Housing partly offset them. This is a change in cash paid, rather than evidence of an overspend against budget.
highways_note: Within City Operations, Birmingham Highways payments increased from £20.63m to £87.58m. A £12m credit also required reconciliation. I would ask City Operations to confirm the contract payment schedule and credit before treating the increase as a continuing cost pressure.
suppliers_intro: I then checked supplier concentration and agency-staff expenditure. These checks help Finance identify where a small number of suppliers or a growing expenditure category warrants a closer review.
supplier_note: The top ten suppliers received 40.5% of the financial year’s payment value. Agency-staff payments rose 28.8% over the matched year-to-date period. Concentration is a prompt to review contract and service context; it does not establish poor value for money.
duplicates_intro: My initial SQL check matched the same supplier and the same payment amount of at least £1,000, within three days. It returned 6,553 payment pairs. Repeated care-package amounts could create legitimate matches, so I refined the screening rule in Python before preparing the AP review list.
duplicate_rules: Match the supplier identifier, rather than relying on a similar name.
Keep the check focused on exact-value payment matches above the screening threshold.
That supplier–amount combination appears exactly twice
Exclude combinations repeated throughout the dataset, which can reflect recurring care-package payments.
No more than three days apart
Retain closely timed pairs; identify same-day matches for the first review pass.
duplicates_result: The refined rule identified 281 candidate pairs worth £4.45m, including 73 paid on the same day. I would start the invoice review with those 73 pairs. The amount represents one potentially repeated payment per pair, rather than the sum of both payments or a confirmed loss.
duplicates_limit: This refinement makes the review list more selective. It can still miss duplicates among recurring amounts, below £1,000 or more than three days apart. It can also flag legitimate transactions. Invoice references and AP investigation are needed to confirm the outcome.
privacy_intro: While checking the publication fields, I found a separate information-governance issue: identifiers on redacted payments also appeared beside names elsewhere in the published data. This linked 213 redacted payment records across 12 identifiers. I report only the aggregate finding here.
privacy_action: I pseudonymised identifiers for personal-data rows and replaced the display names in the reporting dataset. I would refer the publication issue to Information Governance so they could review how records are released together, rather than checking each redacted row in isolation.
actions: Check the 73 same-day pairs against invoice and credit references, then review the remaining candidates.
Track reviewed, confirmed, cleared and unresolved pairs; record any recoveries only after confirmation.
Reconcile the highways payment schedule and £12m credit before explaining the year-on-year movement.
Record the reconciled movement and distinguish timing effects from continuing changes.
Investigate the 260 supplier names linked to multiple supplier identifiers before merging or closing records.
Track verified duplicate supplier records and the decisions taken.
Review identifiers on redacted payments and assess links across the publication.
Document the assessment, publication changes and checks before the next release.
delivery: I produced a SQL reporting model, an Excel finance and payment-controls pack, a management summary and a data-quality log. These are completed analytical outputs; the council has not implemented or evaluated the recommendations as part of this portfolio project.
dashboard: The Power BI dashboard will follow the same questions: expenditure trends, supplier and agency-staff concentration, and payment exceptions. Planned filters include reporting period, directorate and supplier. The Excel pack already contains the supporting measures and review tables.
